units.title: The Kitchen and Its Tools
units.blurb: Stations, ranges and ovens, knives and boards, pans and what they are made of, hand tools and machines.

units.title: Working Like a Cook
units.blurb: Measuring by weight, reading and scaling a recipe, mise en place and working clean.

topics.title: The Kitchen and Its Stations
topics.short: A professional kitchen is laid out in stations around the range, ovens, broiler, fryer and cold storage; each machine has one job it does best.
topics.trouble: New cooks think a salamander, a broiler and an oven are the same thing; they heat from different directions.

topics.title: Knives and Their Parts, Boards and Steels
topics.short: Four knives do most of the work: chef's, paring, serrated and boning. Know the tip, edge, heel, spine, bolster and tang, and keep the board from sliding.
topics.trouble: Beginners buy a big block of knives; a good chef's knife, a paring knife and a serrated knife cover nearly everything.

topics.title: Pans and What They Are Made Of
topics.short: Copper and aluminum spread heat fast, stainless resists acid, cast iron and carbon steel hold heat and season; the shape (sauté, saucepan, rondeau, stockpot, sheet pan) fits the job.
topics.trouble: Cooks crowd one small pan or use a thin pan for searing, then blame the stove for gray meat.

topics.title: Measuring and Hand Tools
topics.short: Scales, thermometers, measuring cups and spoons, ladles and scoops by size, sieves, the chinois, the mandoline with its guard, the spider and the fish spatula.
topics.trouble: People trust a thermometer they have never checked; a quick ice-water test tells you if it reads true.

topics.title: Mixers, Blenders, Processors and Circulators
topics.short: The stand mixer's paddle, whisk and hook; blenders and immersion blenders; the food processor; the combi oven and the immersion circulator.
topics.trouble: Cooks use the whisk attachment for bread dough, or fill a blender with hot soup and seal the lid.

topics.title: Measuring by Weight
topics.short: Professional recipes are written in grams or ounces because a cup of flour can weigh anywhere from about 120 to 160 grams; tare the scale and weigh.
topics.trouble: Learners mix up fluid ounces (volume) and ounces (weight); they match only for water and liquids like it.

topics.title: Reading and Scaling a Recipe
topics.short: Read it all twice, find the times and temperatures, then scale with one conversion factor: new yield ÷ old yield.
topics.trouble: People scale salt, spices and baking powder by the full factor in a huge batch and never taste; or forget pans and times change too.

topics.title: Mise en Place and Working Clean
topics.short: "Everything in its place": read, plan, gather, prep and set up your station before the heat goes on, and clean as you go.
topics.trouble: Beginners start cooking and then chop, so the garlic burns while they hunt for the onion.
